Saint Basil the Great, Archbishop of Cae.life: Saint Basil the Great was Archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia and one of the three Great Hierarchs. He defended the Nicene faith against Arianism, ordered monastic life through his ascetical rules, composed the Divine Liturgy that bears his name, and founded the Basiliad, an early hospital and almshouse. He reposed in 379.
Saint Basil the Great, Archbishop of Cae.patron: Invoked for the sick and the poor; remembered for his charity and learning.
Saint Basil the Great, Archbishop of Cae.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America; the Great Synaxaristes.

Saint Nicholas the Wonderworker, Archbis.life: Archbishop of Myra in Lycia, renowned for his secret almsgiving, his defense of the Nicene faith, and his protection of the wrongly condemned. Countless miracles are attributed to him in life and after his repose, and his relics, translated to Bari in 1087, stream healing myrrh. He is among the most beloved saints of the Church.
Saint Nicholas the Wonderworker, Archbis.patron: Patron of sailors, travelers, children, and the falsely accused; invoked for those in need and danger.
Saint Nicholas the Wonderworker, Archbis.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America; the Great Synaxaristes.

Repose of Venerable Seraphim, Wonderwork.life: Saint Seraphim of Sarov was a beloved Russian monk and hermit known for asceticism and unceasing prayer. After years of solitude he received gifts of clairvoyance and healing, greeting visitors with “My joy, Christ is risen!” He counseled thousands in repentance and peace, and reposed in prayer in 1833.
Repose of Venerable Seraphim, Wonderwork.patron: Invoked for joy, repentance, and spiritual guidance; a model of prayer and gentleness.
Repose of Venerable Seraphim, Wonderwork.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America; the Great Synaxaristes.

Saint John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Con.life: Archbishop of Constantinople and one of the three Great Hierarchs, called 'Golden-Mouth' for his eloquence. A fearless preacher and pastor, he expounded the Scriptures, served the poor, and rebuked injustice, for which he was twice exiled. His Divine Liturgy is celebrated throughout the year. He reposed in exile in 407 with the words, 'Glory to God for all things.'
Saint John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Con.patron: Invoked for preachers and orators; a teacher of repentance and almsgiving.
Saint John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Con.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America; the Great Synaxaristes.

Venerable Mary of Egypt.life: A harlot of Alexandria who, prevented by an unseen power from entering the church in Jerusalem, repented before the icon of the Theotokos and withdrew into the desert beyond the Jordan. There she lived forty-seven years in extreme asceticism, attaining great holiness. Discovered by the elder Zosimas, she received Communion and reposed soon after. She is the supreme image of repentance.
Venerable Mary of Egypt.patron: A model of repentance and conversion; commemorated on the fifth Sunday of Great Lent.
Venerable Mary of Egypt.src: Life by St Sophronius of Jerusalem; Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Greatmartyr and Healer Panteleimon.life: A young physician of Nicomedia, converted to Christ and taught by the priest Hermolaos. He healed the sick freely in the name of Christ, including those whom pagan doctors could not cure, and gave his wealth to the poor. Denounced under Maximian, he endured many torments unharmed before being beheaded. He is numbered among the Holy Unmercenaries.
Greatmartyr and Healer Panteleimon.patron: Patron of physicians and the sick; invoked for healing of body and soul.
Greatmartyr and Healer Panteleimon.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America; the Great Synaxaristes.

Venerable and God-bearing Father Anthony.life: Saint Anthony was born in 251 at Coma in Egypt, near the Thebaid. After hearing the Gospel, he gave away his inheritance and embraced the ascetic life. Known as the father of monasticism, he lived in the desert, instructed many disciples, and reposed in peace at the age of 105.
Venerable and God-bearing Father Anthony.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Saint Athanasius the Great, Archbishop o.life: Saint Athanasius the Great, Archbishop of Alexandria, defended the Orthodox confession of Christ against Arianism. Remembered with Saint Cyril as a wise teacher of truth, he taught from Scripture and endured exile for the Church. His dogmatic writings strengthened the faithful, and he reposed in the fourth century.
Saint Athanasius the Great, Archbishop o.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Macarius the Great of Egypt.life: Saint Macarius the Great was born in the early fourth century in Ptinapor, Egypt. Widowed soon after marriage, he renounced worldly life and entered the desert. He became a renowned Egyptian ascetic and spiritual father, endured trials and slanders with humility, guided monks, and reposed in the Lord near the end of the fourth century.
Venerable Macarius the Great of Egypt.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Euthymius the Great.life: Saint Euthymius the Great was born in Melitene in Armenia and became a monk from youth. He went to Jerusalem, settled in the Palestinian wilderness, and became a guide of monastics. Honored for holiness, discernment, and miracles, he defended the Orthodox faith after Chalcedon and reposed peacefully in the fifth century.
Venerable Euthymius the Great.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Maximus the Confessor.life: Saint Maximus the Confessor was born in Constantinople and served at the imperial court before becoming a monk. He opposed Monothelitism and confessed that Christ has two wills, divine and human. For this teaching he endured exile and mutilation. He reposed in 662 in Lazica, honored as a defender of Orthodox doctrine.
Venerable Maximus the Confessor.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Saint Gregory the Theologian, Archbishop.life: Saint Gregory the Theologian was born in 329 at Arianzos near Cappadocian Nazianzus. Educated in Nazianzus, Caesarea, Alexandria, and Athens, he became a priest and later served Constantinople against Arian and other heresies. Chosen patriarch at the Second Ecumenical Council, he resigned for peace and reposed at Arianzos in 389.
Saint Gregory the Theologian, Archbishop.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Ephraim the Syrian.life: Saint Ephraim the Syrian, a teacher of repentance, was born at Nisibis in Mesopotamia at the beginning of the fourth century. After conversion of heart, he became a deacon, ascetic, hymnographer, and interpreter of Scripture. He taught at Edessa, composed many spiritual writings, served the poor, and reposed in 373.
Venerable Ephraim the Syrian.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Synaxis of the Ecumenical Teachers and H.life: In eleventh-century Constantinople, Christians disputed which of the three hierarchs was greatest. In 1084, Basil, Gregory, and John appeared to Saint John of Euchaita, saying there was no division among them. Bishop John chose January 30 for their common feast, restoring peace and honoring their united witness.
Synaxis of the Ecumenical Teachers and H.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Great Martyr Theodore the Tyro (Recruit).life: Saint Theodore the Tyro was a recruit in the Roman army at Amasea during Maximian’s persecution. Refusing to sacrifice to idols, he burned a pagan temple and confessed Christ before the governor. After imprisonment and tortures, he was cast into fire and received the martyr’s crown in the early fourth century.
Great Martyr Theodore the Tyro (Recruit).src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.
Great Martyr Theodore the Tyro (Recruit).patron: He is traditionally invoked for the recovery of stolen articles.

Saint Leo the Great, Pope of Rome.life: Saint Leo the Great, Pope of Rome, guided the Church in the fifth century. He defended Orthodox Christology against heresy, and his Tome was received at the Fourth Ecumenical Council in Chalcedon. Remembered as a pastor, theologian, and peacemaker, he also interceded for Rome during invasions and reposed in 461.
Saint Leo the Great, Pope of Rome.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Martyr Photini the Samaritan Woman, her.life: Saint Photini is the Samaritan woman who spoke with Christ at Jacob’s well. After Pentecost she preached the Gospel with her family and companions. Arrested under Nero, she confessed Christ before the emperor. After severe tortures, her sons and fellow martyrs suffered with her, and she received the martyr’s crown in the first century.
Martyr Photini the Samaritan Woman, her.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable John Climacus of Sinai, Author.life: Saint John Climacus entered the Sinai monastery as a young man and lived many years in obedience and solitude. Later chosen as abbot of Sinai, he wrote The Ladder of Divine Ascent, describing the soul’s ascent to God through repentance and virtue. Revered as a teacher of monastics, he reposed in the seventh century.
Venerable John Climacus of Sinai, Author.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Greatmartyr, Victory-bearer, and Wonderw.life: Saint George was a Cappadocian soldier who served in the Roman army under Diocletian. When persecution arose, he confessed Christ openly, gave away his wealth, and refused to worship idols. He endured many tortures and was beheaded at Nicomedia about 303, becoming renowned as victory-bearer and wonderworker.
Greatmartyr, Victory-bearer, and Wonderw.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Apostle and Evangelist Mark.life: Saint Mark was one of the Seventy Apostles and the Evangelist who wrote the second Gospel. A companion of Peter, Paul, and Barnabas, he preached in many places and founded the Church of Alexandria. He suffered for Christ in Egypt and received the martyr’s crown in the first century.
Apostle and Evangelist Mark.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Apostle and Evangelist John the Theologi.life: Saint John the Theologian, son of Zebedee and brother of James, was the beloved disciple of Christ. He witnessed the Transfiguration and stood by the Cross with the Theotokos. He preached the Gospel, wrote the fourth Gospel, epistles, and Revelation, and reposed at Ephesus in extreme old age.
Apostle and Evangelist John the Theologi.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Equal of the Apostles and Emperor Consta.life: Saint Constantine became Roman emperor and ended persecution of Christians through the Edict of Milan. He supported the Church and convened the First Ecumenical Council at Nicaea. His mother, Saint Helen, journeyed to Jerusalem and is connected with the finding of the Life-giving Cross. They reposed in the fourth century.
Equal of the Apostles and Emperor Consta.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Nativity of the Holy Glorious Prophet, F.life: This feast celebrates the birth of Saint John the Forerunner, son of the priest Zachariah and righteous Elizabeth. Announced by the Archangel Gabriel, his birth ended Elizabeth’s barrenness and Zachariah’s silence. John was filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother’s womb and prepared the way for Christ.
Nativity of the Holy Glorious Prophet, F.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Equal-to-the-Apostles Blessed Great Prin.life: Saint Olga was princess of Kyiv and grandmother of Saint Vladimir. After the death of Prince Igor, she governed Rus’ with wisdom. She received holy Baptism with the name Helen and promoted Christianity among her people, though Rus’ was not yet baptized. She reposed in 969.
Equal-to-the-Apostles Blessed Great Prin.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Holy Great Prince Vladimir (Basil in Bap.life: Saint Vladimir, Great Prince of Kyiv, was baptized with the name Basil and brought Orthodox Christianity to Rus’. After examining faiths, he received baptism and ordered the people of Kyiv to be baptized in the Dnieper. Remembered as enlightener of Rus’, he reposed in 1015.
Holy Great Prince Vladimir (Basil in Bap.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Great Martyr Marina (Margaret) of Antioc.life: Saint Marina of Antioch was raised in Pisidian Antioch and confessed Christ as a young woman during Diocletian’s persecution. Refusing marriage to a pagan official and refusing sacrifice to idols, she endured imprisonment and tortures. Strengthened by Christ, she was finally beheaded and received the martyr’s crown in the early fourth century.
Great Martyr Marina (Margaret) of Antioc.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Holy, Glorious Prophet Elijah.life: The holy Prophet Elijah lived in the kingdom of Israel during the reign of Ahab. Zealous for the Lord, he rebuked idolatry, called Israel to repentance, and worked wonders by God’s power. Scripture tells that he was taken up into heaven in a fiery chariot rather than dying in the ordinary manner.
Holy, Glorious Prophet Elijah.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Myrrhbearer and Equal of the Apostles Ma.life: Saint Mary Magdalene followed Christ after He healed her and became one of the myrrh-bearing women. She stood near the Cross, came to the tomb with spices, and was the first to proclaim the Resurrection to the apostles. She preached Christ afterward and reposed in the first century.
Myrrhbearer and Equal of the Apostles Ma.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

The Beheading of the Holy Glorious Proph.life: This solemn feast commemorates the martyrdom of Saint John the Forerunner. He rebuked Herod Antipas for unlawfully taking Herodias, his brother’s wife. Imprisoned for the truth, John was beheaded after Herod’s rash oath at a banquet. The Church honors him as prophet, Baptist, and faithful witness to Christ.
The Beheading of the Holy Glorious Proph.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Repose of Venerable Sergius the Wonderwo.life: Saint Sergius of Radonezh was born Bartholomew and became a monk in the forests north of Moscow. He founded the monastery of the Holy Trinity, taught humility, prayer, and brotherly love, and guided monastics and princes. Renowned as a wonderworker and renewer of Russian monastic life, he reposed in 1392.
Repose of Venerable Sergius the Wonderwo.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Hilarion the Great.life: Saint Hilarion the Great was born in Palestine and studied in Alexandria, where he learned of Saint Anthony. Returning home, he gave away his inheritance and embraced the ascetic life near Gaza. He became a founder of Palestinian monasticism, fled human praise, worked many healings, and reposed in Cyprus in the fourth century.
Venerable Hilarion the Great.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Holy, Glorious Demetrios the Myrrh-gushe.life: Saint Demetrios was a noble Christian of Thessaloniki and an officer under Emperor Maximian. He taught the faith openly and strengthened Christians despite persecution. Imprisoned by the emperor, he blessed Nestor to contest the pagan champion Lyaeus. Demetrios was pierced with spears in prison and received the martyr’s crown about 306.
Holy, Glorious Demetrios the Myrrh-gushe.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.
Holy, Glorious Demetrios the Myrrh-gushe.patron: In Slavic tradition he is especially associated with military courage and defense of the homeland.

Apostle and Evangelist Matthew.life: Saint Matthew was a tax collector called by Christ to become one of the Twelve Apostles. He left his former occupation, followed the Lord, and wrote the Gospel that bears his name. After Pentecost he preached the Gospel in many lands, endured sufferings for Christ, and received the martyr’s crown in the first century.
Apostle and Evangelist Matthew.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Great Martyr Katherine of Alexandria.life: Saint Katherine of Alexandria was a learned young woman of royal lineage who confessed Christ during the persecution of Maximinus. She refuted pagan philosophers, converted many, and refused marriage to the emperor. After imprisonment and tortures, including the broken wheel, she was beheaded and received the martyr’s crown in the early fourth century.
Great Martyr Katherine of Alexandria.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Greatmartyr Barbara and Martyr Juliana,.life: Saint Barbara lived at Heliopolis in Syria during Maximian’s reign. Kept in seclusion by her pagan father, she came to know the true God and confessed Christ. After tortures, she was beheaded by her own father. Saint Juliana, who witnessed her suffering and confessed Christ, was also martyred in the early fourth century.
Greatmartyr Barbara and Martyr Juliana,.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Saint Spyridon the Wonderworker, Bishop.life: Saint Spyridon was a humble shepherd in Cyprus who became Bishop of Tremithus. Married before episcopal service and known for simplicity and mercy, he shepherded the Church with holiness. He attended the First Ecumenical Council and defended the Orthodox faith. Many miracles are attributed to him, and he reposed in the fourth century.
Saint Spyridon the Wonderworker, Bishop.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Hieromartyr Ignatius the God-Bearer, Bis.life: Saint Ignatius the God-Bearer was Bishop of Antioch and a disciple of the apostolic age. Arrested under Emperor Trajan, he was taken toward Rome and wrote letters strengthening the churches in faith, unity, and obedience. He desired to suffer for Christ and was thrown to wild beasts in Rome early in the second century.
Hieromartyr Ignatius the God-Bearer, Bis.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

The Circumcision of our Lord and Savior.life: On the eighth day after His Nativity, the Lord Jesus Christ was circumcised according to the Old Testament Law and received the name Jesus, announced by Gabriel. The Fathers teach that He fulfilled the Law, showed that He truly assumed human flesh, and prefigured Baptism and the New Covenant.
The Circumcision of our Lord and Savior.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Martyr Basil of Ancyra.life: Saint Basil lived under Julian the Apostate and confessed Christ before the governor Saturninus. He was tortured at Ancyra, sent to Constantinople, suspended from a tree, stretched on a rack, beaten, stabbed with red-hot needles, and thrown unharmed into a fiery furnace. Later at Caesarea he was torn apart by lions.
Martyr Basil of Ancyra.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Saint Emilia, Mother of Saint Basil the.life: Saint Emilia, mother of Saint Basil the Great, was the daughter of a martyr and wife of the elder Basil, a lawyer and renowned rhetorician of Caesarea. She bore ten children, five of whom were later numbered among the saints: Basil, Macrina, Gregory of Nyssa, Peter of Sebaste, and Theosebia.
Saint Emilia, Mother of Saint Basil the.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Forefeast of the Theophany of our Lord a.life: The third day of the Forefeast of Theophany falls on January 4. OCA notes that the hymns compare the Nativity with the coming Theophany. The liturgical contrast moves from shepherds marveling at the Child to the Father’s voice proclaiming the only-begotten Son at the Jordan.
Forefeast of the Theophany of our Lord a.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Saint Sylvester, Pope of Rome.life: Saint Sylvester, Bishop of Rome from 314 to 335, was born of Christian parents Rufinus and Justa. He received strangers, sheltered the confessor Bishop Timothy of Antioch, and remained steadfast under arrest. Later he guided the Roman Church, defended the faith in public disputation, and reposed peacefully in old age in 335.
Saint Sylvester, Pope of Rome.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Sylvester of the Kyiv Near Cav.life: Saint Sylvester of the Caves lived in the twelfth century and served as igumen of the Mikhailovsk Vydubitsk monastery at Kyiv. He continued the work of Saint Nestor the Chronicler and wrote nine lives of saints of the Kyiv Caves. The service to the Near Caves Fathers praises his blessedness and miraculous protection against demonic suggestions.
Venerable Sylvester of the Kyiv Near Cav.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Holy Prophet Malachi.life: The Holy Prophet Malachi lived about four hundred years before the Birth of Christ, when the Jews returned from the Babylonian Captivity. The Fathers call him the seal of the prophets, the last of the Old Testament prophets. His book rebukes Israel and foretells Christ, His Forerunner, and the Last Judgment.
Holy Prophet Malachi.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Martyr Gordius at Caesarea, in Cappadoci.life: Saint Gordius was born at Caesarea of Cappadocia into a Christian family near the end of the third century. A brave soldier and centurion, he withdrew to the Sinai desert during persecution to prepare for confession. In 320 he appeared at pagan games, declared himself Christian, endured torments, and was beheaded.
Martyr Gordius at Caesarea, in Cappadoci.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Genevieve of Paris.life: Saint Genevieve was born around 422 at Nanterre near Paris, in Gaul, to wealthy parents Severus and Gerontia. From childhood she desired a life pleasing to God. Known for ascetic discipline, prayer, and care for Paris in danger, she became one of the most beloved saints of the city and reposed in the early sixth century.
Venerable Genevieve of Paris.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Synaxis of the Seventy Apostles.life: The Synaxis of the Seventy Apostles was established to honor equally those sent two by two by the Lord before Him into the cities He would visit. After Pentecost they preached in many lands; some accompanied the Twelve, and many endured prison or martyrdom. OCA notes that historical lists contain discrepancies.
Synaxis of the Seventy Apostles.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Theoctistus, Abbot at Cucomo,.life: Saint Theoctistus lived in the second half of the eighth century, during the iconoclastic persecution. He founded and served as igumen of Cucomo Monastery in Sicily. OCA remembers him as a venerable defender of Orthodoxy in a time when iconoclasts persecuted the faithful, and he reposed in peace after ascetic labor.
Venerable Theoctistus, Abbot at Cucomo,.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Repose of Saint Eustathius I, Archbishop.life: Saint Eustathius I, Archbishop of Serbia, lived in the second half of the thirteenth century under King Stephen Urosh. Born in the Budim diocese to a pious Christian family, he received spiritual formation and became known for ascetic discipline and pastoral wisdom. He governed the Serbian Church and reposed in the Lord.
Repose of Saint Eustathius I, Archbishop.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Eve of the Theophany of our Lord and Sav.life: The Eve of Theophany is the fourth day of the Forefeast, January 5. OCA describes the appointed order of services, including Royal Hours, Vespers, and the Liturgy of Saint Basil when the eve falls on a weekday. The day includes thirteen Vespers readings and is kept as a fast regardless of weekday.
Eve of the Theophany of our Lord and Sav.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Hieromartyr Theopemptus, Bishop of Nicom.life: Saints Theopemptus and Theonas suffered at Nicomedia in 303. Theopemptus, bishop of Nicomedia, denounced idolatry under Diocletian, endured furnace, hunger, thirst, and tortures, and remained unharmed by poisons prepared by the sorcerer Theonas. Theonas believed, was baptized as Synesios, and was buried alive; Theopemptus was beheaded.
Hieromartyr Theopemptus, Bishop of Nicom.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Synkletika of Alexandria.life: Saint Synkletika was a native of Alexandria, born to wealthy parents. From youth she loved virginity, fasting, and prayer, refused marriage, and after her parents’ death distributed her inheritance to the poor. She lived with her sister in a crypt, guided women ascetics by word and deed, endured grave illness, and reposed around 350.
Venerable Synkletika of Alexandria.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Prophet Micah.life: The Holy Prophet Micah was a companion of the Prophet Elias. He foretold the ruin of King Ahab in a war with the Assyrians and was cast into prison for that prophecy. After Ahab’s downfall he was set free. OCA records that the prophet Micah died as a martyr in the ninth century before Christ.
Prophet Micah.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Feast of the Theophany of our Lord and S.life: Theophany reveals the Most Holy Trinity through the Baptism of the Lord. The Father spoke from heaven, the Son was baptized by Saint John the Forerunner, and the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove. OCA traces the feast to apostolic times and emphasizes Baptism as spiritual illumination.
Feast of the Theophany of our Lord and S.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Macarius of Mount Athos.life: Saint Macarius was born in Thessalonica during the reign of Emperor Manuel II Palaiologos. As a young man he went to Vatopedi Monastery on Mount Athos. Later he went to Constantinople, became igumen of the Monastery of the Pantocrator, and served as chaplain to the emperor. He died in 1431 during an epidemic in Chalke.
Venerable Macarius of Mount Athos.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Afterfeast of the Theophany of our Lord.life: The seventh day of the Afterfeast of Theophany falls on January 13. The hymns continue to rejoice in God’s manifestation at Christ’s baptism in the Jordan: the Father’s voice is heard, the Son enters the waters, and the Holy Spirit appears in the form of a dove, revealing the Holy Trinity.
Afterfeast of the Theophany of our Lord.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Synaxis of the Holy Glorious Prophet, Fo.life: On the day after Theophany, the Church honors the one who participated directly in the sacred event: Saint John, Prophet, Forerunner, and Baptist. OCA explains that such synaxes follow great feasts of the Lord and the Theotokos to commemorate those immediately involved. John baptized Christ in the Jordan and witnessed the revelation of the Trinity.
Synaxis of the Holy Glorious Prophet, Fo.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Saint Pakhomios of Keno Lake.life: Saint Pakhomios of Keno Lake is commemorated by OCA on the Saturday after Theophany. He was a disciple and fellow ascetic of Saint Alexander of Oshevensk. After leaving his instructor’s monastery, he lived for many years in ascetic struggle, fasting, and prayer, and was remembered for strictness of life and devotion to God.
Saint Pakhomios of Keno Lake.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Saint Brannock of Braunton.life: Saint Brannock lived in the sixth century and tutored the children of the Welsh ruler Brychan. He joined King Brychan on pilgrimage to venerate the tombs of the Apostles, stayed in Brittany for several years on the return journey, and eventually settled at Braunton in Devon, where he became remembered as a holy man of the British Isles.
Saint Brannock of Braunton.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable George the Chozebite, Abbot.life: Saint George the Chozebite was born on Cyprus near the end of the sixth century. After his parents died, he went to Palestine to venerate the holy places and entered the monastery of Chozeba between the Jordan and Jerusalem. He later became abbot, taught fasting, vigil, and labor by example, and reposed in peace.
Venerable George the Chozebite, Abbot.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Domnica of Constantinople.life: Saint Domnica came from Carthage to Constantinople during the reign of the holy Emperor Theodosius the Great. Patriarch Nectarius baptized her, and she entered a women’s monastery. Through strict and prolonged ascetic labor she attained spiritual perfection, healed the sick, showed power over nature, foretold the future, and departed this life in old age.
Venerable Domnica of Constantinople.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Saint Emilian the Confessor, Bishop of C.life: Saint Emilian, Bishop of Cyzicus, zealously defended the holy icons during the reign of Emperor Leo the Armenian. For his Orthodox confession against iconoclasm he suffered torture and martyrdom in 820. The OCA January entry is brief and notes that his principal feast is kept on August 8.
Saint Emilian the Confessor, Bishop of C.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Martyr Polyeuktos of Melitene in Armenia.life: Saint Polyeuktos was a soldier of Melitene in Armenia, first martyred there for Christ. During the persecutions under Decius and Valerian, his Christian friend Nearkhos strengthened him. After a vision of Christ, Polyeuktos tore up the imperial edict, cast down idols, refused family pleas to apostatize, and was beheaded, receiving baptism in his blood.
Martyr Polyeuktos of Melitene in Armenia.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.
Martyr Polyeuktos of Melitene in Armenia.patron: He is venerated in East and West as a patron of vows and treaties.

Hieromartyr Philip, Metropolitan of Mosc.life: Saint Philip, born Theodore Kolichev in 1507, left Moscow court life for the Solovki Monastery, where he was tonsured and later became igumen. Called to be Metropolitan of Moscow, he courageously rebuked Ivan the Terrible’s cruelty. He was deposed, imprisoned, and strangled by Malyuta Skuratov in 1569.
Hieromartyr Philip, Metropolitan of Mosc.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Prophet Shemaiah (Samaia or Semeias).life: The Prophet Shemaiah lived in the days of King Solomon and his son Rehoboam. When the northern tribes of Israel separated from Judah, he commanded Rehoboam not to wage war against them. Scripture records him as a man of God whose word restrained civil conflict; his name means “God hears.”
Prophet Shemaiah (Samaia or Semeias).src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Saint Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa.life: Saint Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa, younger brother of Basil the Great, was educated in Cappadocia and consecrated bishop in 372. He defended Orthodoxy against Arianism, endured exile, helped complete the Creed at the Second Ecumenical Council, wrote dogmatic works, and reposed in old age soon after a council in Constantinople.
Saint Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Saint Dometian, Bishop of Melitene.life: Saint Dometian lived in the sixth century under Emperor Justin the Younger. Widowed, he became a monk and, at thirty, bishop of Melitene in Armenia. Known for zeal, wisdom, diplomacy and almsgiving, he served his flock, helped avert conflict with Persia, and reposed in 601, glorified by miracles.
Saint Dometian, Bishop of Melitene.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Saint Marcian the Presbyter in Constanti.life: Saint Marcian was born in Rome and educated in Constantinople. After his parents’ death, he used his inheritance to build, restore, and adorn churches. Ordained presbyter and treasurer of the Great Church, he distributed alms, lived without covetousness, healed the sick, cast out demons, and reposed between 472 and 474.
Saint Marcian the Presbyter in Constanti.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Theodosius the Great, the Ceno.life: Saint Theodosius the Great was born in Cappadocia in the fifth century and became founder of cenobitic monasticism. After visiting the Holy Land and receiving Saint Simeon Stylites’ blessing, he lived in a Palestinian cave associated with the Magi. Many disciples gathered around him, and he organized communal monastic life before reposing in the sixth century.
Venerable Theodosius the Great, the Ceno.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Michael the Fool-for-Christ of.life: Blessed Michael of Klops, a nobleman related to Great Prince Demetrius of the Don, embraced foolishness for Christ to avoid human praise. Leaving Moscow in rags, he lived at the Klops Monastery near Novgorod for forty-four years. He read Scripture, practiced severe asceticism, received clairvoyance, denounced vice, helped the hungry, and reposed in 1453.
Venerable Michael the Fool-for-Christ of.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Saint Theodosius of Antioch.life: Saint Theodosius of Antioch left his wealthy family in youth and embraced ascetic life near the Gulf of Isska by Ossos. He wore a hairshirt and chains, labored in fasting, prayer, gardening, and rope-making, and founded the Skupela and Maratonia monasteries. Christians and pagans revered his holy life, and he reposed peacefully in 412.
Saint Theodosius of Antioch.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Martyr Tatiana of Rome, and those who su.life: The Virgin Martyr Tatiana was born to an illustrious Roman family and raised secretly in the Christian faith by her father. She became a deaconess, serving God in fasting, prayer, care for the sick, and help for the needy. Under Alexander Severus she refused sacrifice to idols, endured many tortures, converted witnesses, and was beheaded with her father.
Martyr Tatiana of Rome, and those who su.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Martinian, Abbot of Belozersk.life: Saint Martinian of White Lake, born Michael in 1370 near the Cyrilov Monastery, secretly left home at thirteen to follow Saint Cyril of White Lake. He copied books, was ordained deacon and hieromonk, founded a community on Lake Vozha, governed monasteries, supported truth during Moscow’s troubles, and reposed at age eighty-five.
Venerable Martinian, Abbot of Belozersk.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Martyr Mertius of Mauretania.life: The Holy Martyr Mertius was a soldier in Africa during the reign of Diocletian. When the emperor ordered him to sacrifice to idols, he refused and was handed over to torture. He endured severe torments in silence, was cast into prison, and died there from hunger and his wounds.
Martyr Mertius of Mauretania.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Martyrs Hermylus and Stratonicus of Belg.life: The Holy Martyrs Hermylus and Stratonicus, Slavs by origin, lived in the early fourth century under Emperor Licinius. Hermylus was a deacon at Singidunum, present-day Belgrade, and endured imprisonment and torture for Christ. Stratonicus, a prison guard and secret Christian, confessed when he saw his friend suffer. Both were cast into the Danube and buried by Christians.
Martyrs Hermylus and Stratonicus of Belg.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Irenarchus the Recluse of Rost.life: Saint Irenarchus of Rostov was born into a peasant family in Kondakovo and received the baptismal name Elias. Tonsured at the Rostov Saints Boris and Gleb Monastery in his thirtieth year, he embraced severe ascetic labor, barefoot endurance, prayer, poverty, and reclusion. He bore humiliations patiently, guided others spiritually, and became revered as a holy elder.
Venerable Irenarchus the Recluse of Rost.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Eleazar of Anzersk Island, Sol.life: Saint Eleazar of Anzersk was born in Kozelsk to the merchant Severiukov family and received monastic tonsure at Solovki. Gifted in woodcarving, he later withdrew to Anzersk Island in 1612 for prayer and solitude. Disciples gathered, and he organized a strict skete. He loved books, compiled spiritual collections, foretold his death, and reposed in old age.
Venerable Eleazar of Anzersk Island, Sol.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Leavetaking of the Theophany of our Lord.life: The Leavetaking of Theophany is kept on January 14. The office of the feast is repeated, with liturgical omissions noted by OCA: no Entrance, festal readings, Litya, Blessing of Loaves at Vespers, and no Polyeleos or festal Gospel at Matins. At Liturgy the daily Epistle and Gospel are read.
Leavetaking of the Theophany of our Lord.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Saint Savva I, first Archbishop of Serbi.life: Saint Savva, born Rostislav or Rastko, was the son of Serbian ruler Stephen Nemanya. At seventeen he fled to Mount Athos, became a monk, and helped establish Hilandar Monastery. Consecrated first Archbishop of Serbia at Nicaea in 1219, he organized the Serbian Church, strengthened monastic life and Orthodox order, made pilgrimages, and reposed at Trnovo in 1237.
Saint Savva I, first Archbishop of Serbi.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Holy Monastic Fathers slain at Sinai and.life: The Holy Monastic Fathers of Sinai and Raithu commemorate two massacres of desert ascetics. In the fourth century forty fathers were slain at Mount Sinai and thirty-nine at Raithu; another massacre occurred nearly a century later. These monks lived in strict prayer, gathered for vigil and the Mysteries, and were killed by raiders.
Holy Monastic Fathers slain at Sinai and.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Saint Nino (Nina), Equal of the Apostles.life: Saint Nino of Cappadocia, a relative of Great Martyr George, was raised in Jerusalem and learned of Christ’s Robe in pagan Georgia. The Theotokos appeared to her, gave her a grapevine cross, and sent her to preach. She brought the Gospel to Georgia, converting many, including the royal household, and is honored as Equal of the Apostles.
Saint Nino (Nina), Equal of the Apostles.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Paul of Thebes.life: Saint Paul of Thebes was born in Egypt around 227 and fled to the wilderness during Decius’s persecution. He lived ninety-one years in a mountain cave, praying continually and sustained by dates and bread. Saint Anthony found him near death, buried him with help from lions, and Paul reposed in 341, honored as the first hermit.
Venerable Paul of Thebes.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable John Calabytes “the Hut-Dwelle.life: Saint John the Hut-Dweller was born in Constantinople in the early fifth century to wealthy parents. He secretly became a monk at the monastery of the Unsleeping Ones in Bithynia, then returned home disguised as a beggar. Living three years in a hut by his parents’ gate, he revealed himself before death and reposed before age twenty-five.
Venerable John Calabytes “the Hut-Dwelle.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Pansophius of Alexandria, the.life: Saint Pansophius, son of the Alexandrian proconsul Nilus, gave his inheritance to the poor after his father’s death and lived twenty-seven years in desert asceticism. During Decius’s persecution, he was tried before the prefect of Alexandria, confessed Christ, denounced pagan errors, was beaten with rods, and died from the blows around 249 to 251.
Venerable Pansophius of Alexandria, the.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Saint Prochorus, Abbot in the Vranski De.life: Saint Prochorus of Pshina pursued asceticism in the wilderness by the River Pshina and founded a monastery there. The OCA remembers him as one of the great ascetics of monastic life. He died at the end of the tenth century, and miracles occurred from his relics; Serbian tradition says King Milutin later built a church in his honor.
Saint Prochorus, Abbot in the Vranski De.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Veneration of the Precious Chains of the.life: This feast commemorates the chains with which the Apostle Peter was bound when Herod Agrippa imprisoned him about the year 42. According to Acts 12, an angel freed Peter from prison. Christians preserved the chains, and the OCA account says the faithful received healings through them before their later translation to Constantinople and Rome.
Veneration of the Precious Chains of the.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Blessed Maximus the Fool for Christ of T.life: Blessed Maximus Makar'ev was a priest in Tot'ma in the Vologda Diocese during the first half of the seventeenth century. For forty-five years he voluntarily bore the difficult exploit of foolishness for Christ, living in prayer, fasting, and neglect of bodily comfort. He reposed on January 16, 1650, and miracles continued at his tomb.
Blessed Maximus the Fool for Christ of T.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Martyred brothers Speusippus, Eleusippus.life: The brothers Speusippus, Eleusippus, and Meleusippus, with their grandmother Leonilla and companions Neon, Turbo, and Jonilla, suffered in the second century under Marcus Aurelius. Converted through Leonilla’s baptism and confession, the triplets rejected idols and endured hanging, flogging, and fire. Leonilla, Jonilla, Neon, and Turbo also confessed Christ and received martyrdom.
Martyred brothers Speusippus, Eleusippus.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Martyr Danax the Reader, in Macedonia.life: Saint Danax lived in the second century and served as reader in a church at Auleneia in Macedonia. During a pagan invasion, he took the holy vessels of the church to hide them, but soldiers seized him. When he refused to worship their idols, he was killed by being stabbed with a sword.
Martyr Danax the Reader, in Macedonia.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Anthony of Dymsk, Novgorod.life: Saint Anthony of Dymsk was born at Novgorod about 1157. Hearing Christ’s call to take up the cross, he entered monastic life under Saint Barlaam of Khutyn. After serving as igumen, he withdrew to Lake Dyma near Tikhvin, founded a monastery, struggled there until his repose on June 24, 1224, and his incorrupt relics were found in 1330.
Venerable Anthony of Dymsk, Novgorod.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Anthony of Chernoezero.life: Saint Anthony of Chernoezero, or Black Lake, founded the Mother of God monastery at Black Lake in the Novgorod region, near Chernopovets. The monastery stood on an island in the Schirsk countryside. The OCA account records its later destruction by Lithuanians in 1581 and Swedes in 1682, and its closing in 1764.
Venerable Anthony of Chernoezero.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Saint Anthony of Krasny Kholm.life: Saint Anthony of Krasny Kholm was a hieromonk and wilderness-dweller near White Lake. He later came to the Tver region and settled by the River Mologa near Krasny Kholm, building a chapel and cell. After an icon of Saint Nicholas was found, a stone church and monastery arose there, and he guided the brethren until his death in 1481.
Saint Anthony of Krasny Kholm.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Saint Cyril, Archbishop of Alexandria.life: Saint Cyril, Archbishop of Alexandria, was educated by his uncle Patriarch Theophilus and succeeded him in 412. A defender of the Orthodox Faith, he opposed Nestorian teaching and presided at the Third Ecumenical Council in 431, where the blasphemy against the Most Holy Theotokos was censured. After resuming his see following intrigue, he reposed in 444.
Saint Cyril, Archbishop of Alexandria.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Athanasius, Abbot of Syandemsk.life: Saint Athanasius of Syandemsk and Vologda was a disciple of Saint Alexander of Svir. After his mentor’s death he established the Dormition hermitage in the forests of Karelia on Lake Syandem. Later chosen igumen of the Svir monastery, he returned to his hermitage, reposed about 1550 in great old age, and his incorrupt relics were placed in church in 1720.
Venerable Athanasius, Abbot of Syandemsk.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Righteous Athanasius of Novolotsk.life: Righteous Athanasius of Novolotsk came at the end of the sixteenth century from the Kargopol region to the Olonets land. There he founded a monastery seventy-eight versts from the place that later became Petrozavodsk. The OCA account gives few details of his life and says that he died at a Verkholedsk suburb near Shenkursk.
Righteous Athanasius of Novolotsk.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Macarius of Alexandria.life: Saint Macarius of Alexandria was born in 295 and worked in trade until about forty. After baptism he withdrew to the desert for more than sixty years. Ordained priest, he became head of the Cells between Nitria and Skete, imitated severe ascetic labors, resisted vainglory, worked miracles, and was a contemporary and friend of Macarius of Egypt.
Venerable Macarius of Alexandria.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Saint Mark, Archbishop of Ephesus.life: Saint Mark Eugenikos, Archbishop of Ephesus, defended Orthodoxy at the Council of Florence. He rejected union with Rome based on theological compromise and political expediency, answered opponents from the teaching of the Fathers, and alone refused to sign the Tomos of Union. Returning to Constantinople, he urged repudiation of the document and reposed in 1457 at fifty-two.
Saint Mark, Archbishop of Ephesus.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Macarius the Faster, of the Ky.life: Saint Macarius the Faster of the Kyiv Near Caves was a deacon among the ascetics of the Kyiv Caves. The OCA account says he is commemorated on January 19 because of his namesake, Saint Macarius of Egypt. He is also commemorated on September 28 and in the general remembrance of the Kyiv Caves wonderworkers on the second Sunday of Great Lent.
Venerable Macarius the Faster, of the Ky.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Euthymius the Schemamonk.life: Saint Euthymius the Schemamonk of the Kyiv Caves imposed on himself a vow of silence, opening his mouth only for church services and prayer. The OCA account says the silent schemamonk ate only herbs and was buried in the Far Caves of Saint Theodosius at the Kyiv Caves monastery. He is also commemorated on August 28 and the second Sunday of Great Lent.
Venerable Euthymius the Schemamonk.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Saint Laurence, Recluse of the Kyiv Far.life: Saint Laurence, Recluse of the Kyiv Far Caves, renounced the vain glory of this world and lived enclosed in a cave. The OCA notice says he conquered the passions through prayer and fasting. His incorrupt relics rest in the Far Caves of the Kyiv Caves Lavra, where he is remembered among the ascetics of that holy monastery.
Saint Laurence, Recluse of the Kyiv Far.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Euthymius of Syanzhemsk, Volog.life: Saint Euthymius of Syanzhemsk and Vologda was born in Vologda and received monastic tonsure at the Savior-Stone monastery on Lake Kuben. After living in solitude by the River Kuben, he moved to Syanzhem, founded the Ascension monastery, and became its igumen. He appointed Saint Chariton as successor and reposed around 1465.
Venerable Euthymius of Syanzhemsk, Volog.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Martyr Neophytus of Nicea.life: Saint Neophytus of Nicea in Bithynia was raised in Christian piety and received the gift of wonderworking as a child. Led by a dove to a cave on Mount Olympus, he lived there from age nine to fifteen. During Diocletian’s persecution he denounced pagan impiety, endured torture and a red-hot oven unharmed, and was killed by sword or spear at sixteen.
Martyr Neophytus of Nicea.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Martyrs Eugene, Candidus, Valerian, and.life: Saints Eugene, Candidus, Valerian, and Aquila suffered near Trebizond during the reigns of Diocletian and Maximian under the commander Lycius. Valerian, Candidus, and Aquila hid in the hills rather than live with pagans, but were found and tortured. Eugene was later arrested and tormented with them. After emerging unharmed from a red-hot oven, all four were beheaded.
Martyrs Eugene, Candidus, Valerian, and.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Virgin Martyr Agnes of Rome.life: Saint Agnes of Rome was born in the third century to Christian parents and dedicated herself to virginity from youth. Refusing marriage and pagan worship, she was threatened with public shame, but God protected her. After miracles led many to faith, she endured torture; fire did not harm her, and she was killed by a sword thrust to the throat at age thirteen.
Virgin Martyr Agnes of Rome.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Apostle Timothy of the Seventy.life: The holy Apostle Timothy was from Lystra in Lycaonia and was converted to Christ by the Apostle Paul in the year 52. He became Paul’s beloved disciple and co-worker and was appointed Bishop of Ephesus. Zealous for Christ, he rebuked an idolatrous procession and was beaten, dragged, and stoned to death in 93.
Apostle Timothy of the Seventy.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Apostle Timothy of the Seventy.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Monastic Martyr Anastasius the Persian.life: Saint Anastasius the Persian, formerly the pagan soldier Magundates, learned of Christ after seeing the power of the Holy Cross taken from Jerusalem. Baptized Anastasius, he became a monk in a Jerusalem monastery. Arrested at Caesarea, he refused to deny Christ under torture and was strangled and beheaded by order of Chozroes in the seventh century.
Monastic Martyr Anastasius the Persian.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Monastic Martyr Anastasius the Persian.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Monastic Martyr Anastasius the Deacon of.life: Saint Anastasius the Deacon lived an ascetical life in the Kyiv Near Caves. Manuscript traditions identify him as a deacon and brother of Saint Titus the Presbyter. The OCA notes that the Synaxis service praises his courage before torturers, his boldness before God, and his power to drive away evil spirits.
Monastic Martyr Anastasius the Deacon of.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Monastic Martyr Anastasius the Deacon of.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Macarius of Zhabyn the Wonderw.life: Saint Macarius of Zhabyn, Wonderworker of Belev, was born in 1539 and first tonsured with the name Onuphrius. In 1585 he founded Zhabyn’s Entry of the Theotokos Monastery near the Oka River. He restored the monastery after devastation, lived in severe asceticism, healed the sick, and reposed in 1623.
Venerable Macarius of Zhabyn the Wonderw.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Venerable Macarius of Zhabyn the Wonderw.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Hieromartyr Clement, Bishop of Ancyra, a.life: The Hieromartyr Clement was born in Ancyra in Galatia in 258 to a pagan father and Christian mother. Raised by Sophia after being orphaned, he served the Church and became Bishop of Ancyra at twenty. Under Diocletian and Maximian he endured many tortures with Agathangelus; Clement was beheaded while celebrating Liturgy on January 23.
Hieromartyr Clement, Bishop of Ancyra, a.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Hieromartyr Clement, Bishop of Ancyra, a.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Gennadius of Kostroma.life: Saint Gennadius of Kostroma, born Gregory in Mogilev, left a wealthy family for monastic life. Tonsured by Saint Cornelius of Komel, he helped found the Transfiguration monastery near Lake Sura about 1529 and became its igumen. Known for ascetic labor, icon painting, clairvoyance, and wonderworking, he reposed on January 23, 1565.
Venerable Gennadius of Kostroma.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Venerable Gennadius of Kostroma.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Translation of the relics of Saint Theoc.life: This commemoration honors the transfer of the relics of Saint Theoctistus, Archbishop of Novgorod. His principal feast is December 23. OCA records that he was glorified in 1664 because healings occurred at his relics. In 1786 the relics were moved to Yuriev, where Archimandrite Photius built a chapel in his honor.
Translation of the relics of Saint Theoc.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Translation of the relics of Saint Theoc.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Mausimas the Syrian.life: Saint Mausimas the Syrian lived near Cyrrhus in Syria. He freely embraced poverty and devoted himself to serving his neighbor, keeping his hut open to all in need. Bread and oil were always available there, and the vessels were not exhausted. After this life of mercy and ascetic simplicity, he reposed at the end of the fourth century.
Venerable Mausimas the Syrian.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Venerable Mausimas the Syrian.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Xenia of Rome, and her two fem.life: Saint Xenia of Rome, born Eusebia, was the only daughter of a Roman senator. Avoiding an arranged marriage, she left with two servants and settled at Milassa in Caria. She founded a church and women’s monastery, was made deaconess by Bishop Paul, served the needy, and reposed while praying in 450.
Venerable Xenia of Rome, and her two fem.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Venerable Xenia of Rome, and her two fem.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Saint Gerasimus, Bishop of Perm.life: Saint Gerasimus, Bishop of Great Perm and Ust-Vymsk, led the newly enlightened Zyryani people after 1416. He took part in Moscow councils opposing the Union of Florence and interceded for his flock before Great Prince Basil II. During a journey through Perm in 1441, he was murdered by a Vogulian servant and buried at Ust-Vyma.
Saint Gerasimus, Bishop of Perm.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Saint Gerasimus, Bishop of Perm.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Martyr John of Kazan.life: Saint John of Kazan was among Russians taken captive to Kazan after Tatar raids under Great Prince Basil. Given to Alei-Shnura, he served faithfully by day, prayed by night, and refused to renounce Christ. In 1529 he was mortally wounded, received the Holy Mysteries from a priest, prayed through the night, and died the next morning.
Martyr John of Kazan.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Martyr John of Kazan.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Martyr Babylas of Sicily, and his two di.life: The Martyrs Babylas of Sicily and his disciples Timothy and Agapius lived in the third century near Rome. Babylas left his wealthy home for ascetic life on a mountain, and his disciples labored with him. Fleeing persecution to Sicily, they converted many to Christ, were tortured by the governor, and died by the sword.
Martyr Babylas of Sicily, and his two di.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Martyr Babylas of Sicily, and his two di.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

New Martyrs and Confessors of Russia.life: This Synaxis remembers Orthodox Christians who suffered for Christ under Soviet persecution. OCA names among them the royal Passion Bearers, Grand Duchess Elizabeth, hierarchs, clergy, monastics, and lay faithful. Many were killed, while confessors endured prisons, camps, exile, and torment without death, bearing witness to Christ in the twentieth century.
New Martyrs and Confessors of Russia.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
New Martyrs and Confessors of Russia.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Theodosius, Abbot of Totma, Vo.life: Saint Theodosius of Totma was born at Vologda about 1530 and was raised in Christian piety. After the deaths of his parents and wife, he entered the Priluki Monastery and later founded a monastery near Totma. He labored in poverty, prayer, and humility, became known for holiness, and reposed in 1568.
Venerable Theodosius, Abbot of Totma, Vo.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Venerable Theodosius, Abbot of Totma, Vo.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Ephraim the Wonderworker, Abbo.life: Saint Ephraim of Novy Torg was a native of Hungary and brother of Saints Moses the Hungarian and George. After George was killed, Ephraim left worldly life, embraced monasticism, and founded the Saints Boris and Gleb Monastery at Novy Torg. He became known as a wonderworker and reposed in 1053.
Venerable Ephraim the Wonderworker, Abbo.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Venerable Ephraim the Wonderworker, Abbo.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Translation of the relics of the Hieroma.life: This feast commemorates the transfer of Saint Ignatius’s relics after his martyrdom in Rome under Trajan in 107. Christians preserved his bones, buried them outside Daphne at Antioch in 108, and later brought them into Antioch. OCA also notes later returns to Rome and his teaching on unity around the bishop.
Translation of the relics of the Hieroma.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Translation of the relics of the Hieroma.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Saint Laurence, Recluse of the Kyiv Cave.life: Saint Laurence first lived as a hermit near the Kyiv Caves, at the monastery of the Great Martyr Demetrius. He later moved to the Kyiv Caves Monastery and was glorified with a gift of healing. Elevated as Bishop of Turov in 1182, he died in 1194 and was buried in the Near Caves.
Saint Laurence, Recluse of the Kyiv Cave.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Saint Laurence, Recluse of the Kyiv Cave.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Saint Pitirim, Bishop of Perm.life: Saint Pitirim succeeded Saint Gerasimus as Bishop of Great Perm and Ustiug. He defended the Zyryan flock against attacks, appealed to the Great Prince in 1447, traveled widely to instruct Christians and enlighten the pagan Voguli, and converted many. He was murdered by the Vogul leader Asyk while serving a Molieben in 1455.
Saint Pitirim, Bishop of Perm.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Saint Pitirim, Bishop of Perm.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Martyr Agatha of Palermo in Sicily.life: The holy Virgin Martyr Agatha was born to respected Christian parents in Palermo, Sicily. During Decius’s persecution, the prefect Quintianus had her seized and brought to Catania. She rejected pagan sacrifice, endured cruel tortures, was healed in prison by the Apostle Peter, and peacefully surrendered her soul to the Lord.
Martyr Agatha of Palermo in Sicily.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Martyr Agatha of Palermo in Sicily.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Repose of Saint Theodosius of Chernihiv.life: Saint Theodosius, Archbishop of Chernihiv, was born in the seventeenth century in the Podolsk region and educated at Kyiv’s Brotherhood Theophany school. Tonsured at the Kyiv Caves Lavra, he served as igumen and hierarch, restored monasteries, guided clergy and flock, reposed on February 5, 1696, and was glorified in 1896.
Repose of Saint Theodosius of Chernihiv.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Repose of Saint Theodosius of Chernihiv.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Martyr Theodula of Anazarbus, and the Ma.life: Saint Theodula lived in Anazarbus of Asia Minor under Diocletian and Maximian. Brought before the cruel prefect Pelagius, she confessed Christ and refused idol worship. Through her prayers and endurance, Helladius, Macarius, Evagrius, and many others believed. They were cast into a heated oven and received the crown of martyrdom.
Martyr Theodula of Anazarbus, and the Ma.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Martyr Theodula of Anazarbus, and the Ma.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Saint Bucolus, Bishop of Smyrna.life: Saint Bucolus, a disciple of Apostle and Evangelist John the Theologian, became the first Bishop of Smyrna in Asia Minor. He converted and baptized many pagans, protected his flock from heresy, and entrusted them to Saint Polycarp. He reposed peacefully between 100 and 105; a healing myrtle grew at his grave.
Saint Bucolus, Bishop of Smyrna.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Saint Bucolus, Bishop of Smyrna.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Saint Photius, Patriarch of Constantinop.life: Saint Photius, born into a zealous Christian family, became Patriarch of Constantinople in the ninth century after brilliant service as a scholar and imperial secretary. He defended Orthodox faith against papal claims and the Latin Filioque, supported the mission to the Slavs, suffered deposition and imprisonment, and reposed in 891.
Saint Photius, Patriarch of Constantinop.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Saint Photius, Patriarch of Constantinop.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Barsanuphius the Great and Joh.life: Saints Barsanuphius the Great and John the Prophet lived in sixth-century Palestine at the monastery of Abba Seridus near Gaza. Barsanuphius embraced long seclusion, prayer, fasting, silence, and discernment; John, his disciple, became known for clairvoyance. Their answers guided monks and later generations. OCA notes Barsanuphius’s repose is dated either 563 or before 600.
Venerable Barsanuphius the Great and Joh.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Venerable Barsanuphius the Great and Joh.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Saint Parthenios, Bishop of Lampsakos.life: Saint Parthenios was from Melitopolis in Asia Minor, the son of Deacon Christopher. Though unable to read as a youth, he learned Scripture through church services and gave generously to the poor. Ordained priest and then Bishop of Lampsakos in Constantine’s reign, he preached Christ, healed the sick freely, cast out demons, and converted many pagans.
Saint Parthenios, Bishop of Lampsakos.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Saint Parthenios, Bishop of Lampsakos.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Luke of Hellas.life: Saint Luke of Hellas was born in Kastorion, Greece, to poor farmers. From childhood he worked, obeyed his parents, fasted, prayed, and gave to the poor. After monastic struggles in Athens, Mount Ioannou, Corinth, Patras, Kalamion, Ampelon, and Steiris, he founded a monastery, healed many, foresaw his end, and reposed on February 7, 946.
Venerable Luke of Hellas.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Venerable Luke of Hellas.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

1,003 Martyrs of Nicomedia.life: The 1,003 Martyrs of Nicomedia were servants of Bassos, Eusebius, Eutychius, and Basilides, who had suffered for Christ with their wives in 303 under Diocletian. After their masters’ martyrdom, the servants likewise confessed themselves Christians. Neither threats nor rewards moved them, and men, women, and children were slain by soldiers.
1,003 Martyrs of Nicomedia.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
1,003 Martyrs of Nicomedia.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Greatmartyr Theodore Stratelates “the Ge.life: Saint Theodore Stratelates came from Euchaita in Asia Minor and served as a commander in Heraklea. Enlightened in the Christian faith, he slew a dragon, confessed Christ before Emperor Licinius, and endured cruel tortures. Strengthened by Christ and refusing idolatry, he was beheaded at Heraklea in 319.
Greatmartyr Theodore Stratelates “the Ge.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Greatmartyr Theodore Stratelates “the Ge.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Prophet Zachariah.life: Prophet Zachariah the Sickle-Seer was the eleventh of the Twelve Minor Prophets. Descended from Levi and apparently a priest, he was called young to prophecy after the Babylonian exile. His visions and sayings encouraged the rebuilding of the Temple and foretold mysteries of Christ; he died in the sixth century before Christ.
Prophet Zachariah.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Prophet Zachariah.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Saint Sava II, Archbishop of Serbia.life: Saint Sava II, born Predislav Nemanjić, was son of Saint-King Stephen the First-Crowned and nephew of Saint Sava I. He distinguished himself in monastic asceticism and succeeded Saint Arsenius as Archbishop of Serbia in 1266. He guided the Church with love and dedication until his repose, variously dated 1268, 1269, or 1271.
Saint Sava II, Archbishop of Serbia.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Saint Sava II, Archbishop of Serbia.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Leavetaking of the Meeting of our Lord i.life: The Leavetaking of the Meeting of the Lord usually falls on February 9, though it may move if the feast falls during the Triodion. On this day the Church concludes the celebration of Christ’s presentation in the Temple, repeating most of the festal office and returning the commemoration liturgically to ordinary time.
Leavetaking of the Meeting of our Lord i.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Leavetaking of the Meeting of our Lord i.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Martyr Nikephoros of Antioch, in Syria.life: Saint Nikephoros lived in Syrian Antioch and had been close to the presbyter Sapricius before a quarrel separated them. Seeking reconciliation, Nikephoros humbled himself, but Sapricius refused forgiveness. When Sapricius apostatized at execution, Nikephoros confessed Christ in his place and was beheaded, receiving the martyr’s crown.
Martyr Nikephoros of Antioch, in Syria.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Martyr Nikephoros of Antioch, in Syria.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Uncovering of the relics of Saint Innoce.life: The first Bishop of Irkutsk, Saint Innocent reposed in 1731. His incorrupt body was found in 1764, and on February 9, 1805, the Holy Synod ordered his relics uncovered and numbered him among the saints. Later seized during persecution, his relics were rediscovered in Yaroslavl in 1990 and returned to Irkutsk.
Uncovering of the relics of Saint Innoce.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Uncovering of the relics of Saint Innoce.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Pancratius of the Kyiv Caves.life: Saint Pancratius of the Kyiv Caves was a holy hieromonk of the monastery’s ascetic tradition. He served the divine services with much grace and received the gift of working miracles. Sharing his gifts freely with those who asked, he healed the sick through fasting, prayer, and anointing with holy oil. His date of repose is not specified.
Venerable Pancratius of the Kyiv Caves.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Venerable Pancratius of the Kyiv Caves.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Hieromartyr Haralambos, Bishop of Magnes.life: Saint Haralambos, Bishop of Magnesia in Asia Minor, preached Christ during the reign of Septimius Severus and was arrested with Porphyrius, Baptus, and three women martyrs. Though 113 years old, he endured tortures, healed persecutors by prayer, and strengthened many witnesses. He died before beheading in 202 and was buried by Galina.
Hieromartyr Haralambos, Bishop of Magnes.patron: In his final prayer he asked that the place where his relics repose be spared famine and disease.
Hieromartyr Haralambos, Bishop of Magnes.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Synaxis of the Hierarchs of Novgorod, Bu.life: The Synaxis of the Novgorod Hierarchs commemorates holy bishops and archbishops connected with the Cathedral of Holy Wisdom in Novgorod. OCA records that Saint John appeared in 1439 to Saint Euthymius, ordering memorial prayer for those buried there. The synaxis later marked their glorification and is also celebrated on October 4 and after Pentecost.
Synaxis of the Hierarchs of Novgorod, Bu.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Synaxis of the Hierarchs of Novgorod, Bu.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Princess Anna of Novgorod.life: Princess Anna of Novgorod, wife of Great Prince Yaroslav the Wise, formed her children in Christian faith, diligence, integrity, and learning. Her son Mstislav became Great Prince of Kyiv, and a daughter became a western queen. Renouncing worldly life, Anna entered a monastery and ended her days in strict obedience and prayer in 1056.
Princess Anna of Novgorod.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Princess Anna of Novgorod.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Prochorus of the Kyiv Near Cav.life: Saint Prochorus, a native of Smolensk, entered the Kyiv Caves monastery under Igumen John. A strict ascetic, he ate pigweed bread and drank water, and by God’s grace his bread fed the needy during famine. He also turned ashes into salt by prayer. He reposed in 1107 and was buried in the Near Caves.
Venerable Prochorus of the Kyiv Near Cav.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Venerable Prochorus of the Kyiv Near Cav.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Hieromartyr Blaise, Bishop of Sebaste.life: Saint Blaise, Bishop of Sebaste, lived during the persecutions of Diocletian and Licinius. Chosen for his righteous life, he strengthened prisoners and martyrs, later living in a cave on Mount Argeos where he healed animals. Arrested by Governor Agrilaus, he confessed Christ through tortures and was beheaded with two boys around 316.
Hieromartyr Blaise, Bishop of Sebaste.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Hieromartyr Blaise, Bishop of Sebaste.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Venerable Demetrios, Wonderworker of Pri.life: Saint Demetrios of Priluki was born in Pereyaslavl-Zalessk and became a monk and igumen. A friend of Saint Sergius of Radonezh, he founded the Savior monastery near Vologda, lived in strict asceticism, fed the poor, welcomed strangers, and counseled the troubled. He reposed peacefully on February 11, 1392, and miracles followed from his relics.
Venerable Demetrios, Wonderworker of Pri.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Venerable Demetrios, Wonderworker of Pri.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Saint Vsevolod (in Baptism Gabriel), Won.life: Saint Vsevolod of Pskov, baptized Gabriel, was a grandson of Vladimir Monomakh and son of Saint Mstislav. As prince in Novgorod and later Pskov, he built churches, granted privileges to Holy Wisdom, defended his people, and spent his treasury during famine. He endured exile, reposed in 1138, and remained a wonderworker of Pskov.
Saint Vsevolod (in Baptism Gabriel), Won.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Saint Vsevolod (in Baptism Gabriel), Won.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Righteous Theodora, wife of Emperor Theo.life: Holy Empress Theodora was wife of Emperor Theophilus the Iconoclast but secretly venerated the holy icons. After his death she governed for her minor son Michael, convened a council, anathematized the Iconoclasts, and restored icon veneration, establishing the Triumph of Orthodoxy. Later she retired to Saint Euphrosynē’s monastery and reposed peacefully around 867.
Righteous Theodora, wife of Emperor Theo.patron: No specific patronage is attested in the consulted Orthodox source.
Righteous Theodora, wife of Emperor Theo.src: Lives of the Saints, Orthodox Church in America.

Martyr Tathuil, and his sister, Bebaia.life: The Holy Martyrs Tathuil and his sister Bebaia suffered for Christ at Edessa in the days of the emperor Hadrian, for their bold and fruitful preaching of the Gospel among the pagans. Tathuil, whom some accounts name Thiphael, had turned from the service of the idols to the true God, and by his words many were brought to the faith;.
Martyr Tathuil, and his sister, Bebaia.patron: Invoked for bold preaching; steadfast confession.
Martyr Tathuil, and his sister, Bebaia.src: Adapted from the Synaxarion (Lives of the Saints).

Uncovering of the relics of Saint Gurias.life: On this day the Church commemorates the uncovering of the relics of Saint Gurias, first Archbishop of Kazan, and Saint Barsanuphius, Bishop of Tver, which took place at Kazan in the year 1595, when a new stone church of the Transfiguration was being built at the monastery Barsanuphius had founded, and the graves of the two hierarchs were found beneath the old wooden church.
Uncovering of the relics of Saint Gurias.src: Adapted from the Synaxarion (Lives of the Saints).

Greatmartyr Paraskevi of Iconium.life: The Holy Great Martyr Paraskevi of Iconium lived in the third century, born to a rich and devout family who held in special reverence the Friday of the Lord's Passion, and therefore named their daughter Paraskevi, which means Friday. Loving purity from her youth, she vowed her virginity to Christ and, when her parents reposed, gave her wealth to the poor and devoted herself to enlightening the pagans of her city with the light of the Gospel.
Greatmartyr Paraskevi of Iconium.src: Adapted from the Synaxarion (Lives of the Saints).

Saint Maximus, Metropolitan of Kyiv.life: Saint Maximus, Metropolitan of Kyiv and All Rus, a Greek by birth, was sent from Constantinople in 1283 to shepherd the Church of Rus in the deep night of the Tatar yoke, when Kyiv, twice devastated, lay half in ruins and the metropolitan's own court could scarcely be maintained amid the desolation.
Saint Maximus, Metropolitan of Kyiv.patron: Invoked for hierarchs; the shepherding of a devastated land.
Saint Maximus, Metropolitan of Kyiv.src: Adapted from the Synaxarion (Lives of the Saints).

Martyrs Theodore and his son, John, of K.life: The Holy Martyrs Theodore the Varangian and his son John were the first martyrs of the land of Rus, living at Kyiv in the tenth century, in the days before Prince Vladimir embraced the faith. Theodore, a Varangian by descent and a Christian, had returned to Kyiv with his young son John.
Martyrs Theodore and his son, John, of K.src: Adapted from the Synaxarion (Lives of the Saints).

Venerable Auxentius of Bithynia.life: Venerable Auxentius of Bithynia was a Syrian by birth who rose at Constantinople to the equestrian guard of the emperor Theodosius the Younger, a courtier famed in the capital for piety, learning, and a wisdom that churchmen sought out; and at the height of that standing he vanished, crossing the strait to Bithynia and hiding himself as a hermit on the mountain called Oxia near Chalcedon, which bears to this day the name of Mount Saint Auxentius.
Venerable Auxentius of Bithynia.patron: Invoked for cantors; those who teach the people to sing.
Venerable Auxentius of Bithynia.src: Adapted from the Synaxarion (Lives of the Saints).

Saint Alexander, Patriarch of Constantin.life: Saint Alexander was a bishop under Saint Metrophanes, the first patriarch of Constantinople, and because of the great age of Metrophanes he was sent in his place to the First Ecumenical Council at Nicaea, where the Arian heresy was condemned; and upon the repose of Metrophanes, who had named him in his will, Alexander succeeded to the throne of the imperial city.
Saint Alexander, Patriarch of Constantin.src: Adapted from the Synaxarion (Lives of the Saints).

Leavetaking of the Nativity of our Lord.life: The Leavetaking of the Nativity of our Lord, the Apodosis, is kept on the thirty-first of December, and on it the Church sings the feast once more in nearly its whole festal fullness, the hymns and canon of Bethlehem returning in force as at the feast itself, so that the season ends not by fading but by a final blaze, the door of the feast closed from within with singing.
Leavetaking of the Nativity of our Lord.patron: Commemorated in the holy calendar of the Church.
Leavetaking of the Nativity of our Lord.src: Adapted from the Synaxarion (Lives of the Saints).

Martyr Gerontius, and those with him, of.life: The holy new martyrs of the David Gareji monastery in the Georgian wilderness gave their lives for Christ in the summer of the year 1851, when a Dagestani army fell upon that ancient lavra founded by Saint David. The raiders plundered the monastery, carrying off its sacred vessels and books, and took the monks captive, torturing and slaying the most steadfast among them.
Martyr Gerontius, and those with him, of.patron: Invoked for monastics; steadfast confession under persecution.
Martyr Gerontius, and those with him, of.src: Adapted from the Synaxarion (Lives of the Saints).

Martyrs Nikephoros, Antoninus, and Germa.life: The Holy Martyrs Antoninus, Nikephoros, and Germanus suffered at Caesarea in Palestine about the year 308, in the reign of Maximinus, when the governor Firmilian pressed the persecution against the Church with public sacrifices and spectacles. As the pagan rites were being celebrated before the assembled city, the three Christians came forward of their own will and, standing before the governor, rebuked the worship of lifeless idols and confessed with a loud voice the one true God and His Christ;.
Martyrs Nikephoros, Antoninus, and Germa.src: Adapted from the Synaxarion (Lives of the Saints).

Venerable Sebastian of Poshekhonye.life: Venerable Sebastian of Poshekhonye labored about the turn of the sixteenth century in the forest country beyond the Volga, one of the quiet host of founders who, in the generations after Sergius of Radonezh, carried the hermit's lamp northward river by river until the whole wilderness of Russia was strung with monasteries;.
Venerable Sebastian of Poshekhonye.patron: Invoked for founders; hermits of the northern forests.
Venerable Sebastian of Poshekhonye.src: Adapted from the Synaxarion (Lives of the Saints).

Hieromartyr Hermogenes, Patriarch of Mos.life: The Hieromartyr Hermogenes, Patriarch of Moscow and All Russia, was the anchor that held a drowning nation, and he held it from a starvation cell.
